ES.evidence_source: For Study X1 (Fuchs-Beauchamp et al., 1993): "correlations between intelligence and creative potential ranging from r =.19 to r = .49 for a subsample with an IQ below 120. In a subsample above that level, none of the coefficients exceeded r = .12." Detected values: 0.19, 0.49 (for IQ < 120), and <= 0.12 (for IQ > 120). Calculation: Average for IQ < 120 is (0.19 + 0.49) / 2 = 0.34. Assuming the highest value for IQ > 120 is 0.12. Overall average is (0.34 + 0.12) / 2 = 0.23. For Study X2 (Yamamoto, 1964): "a significant correlation between intelligence and creative potential ofr = .30 was found while no significant correlations emerged when gifted children were selected". Detected values: 0.30 (non-gifted), 0.00 (gifted, inferred from 'no significant correlations'). Calculation: Average = (0.30 + 0.00) / 2 = 0.15. For Study X3 (Yamamoto, 1966): "correlations of r = .50 and r = .20 were reported below and above an IQ threshold of 120, respectively". Detected values: 0.50 (below 120), 0.20 (above 120). Calculation: Average = (0.50 + 0.20) / 2 = 0.35. For Study X4 (Cho et al., 2010): "Correlations between intelligence and creative potential of up to r = .40 were observed in an average IQ sample while correlations in the higher IQ sample equaled zero." Detected values: <= 0.40 (average IQ), 0.00 (higher IQ). Calculation: Assuming highest value for average IQ sample is 0.40. Average = (0.40 + 0.00) / 2 = 0.20. For Study X6 (Preckel et al., 2006): "They found correlations between processing capacity and ideational fluency ranging from r = .3 to r = .4 at all levels of cognitive ability." Detected values: 0.3, 0.4. Calculation: Average = (0.3 + 0.4) / 2 = 0.35. For Study X7 (Kim, 2005): "A meta-analysis estimated mean correlations below and above an IQ of 120 to be r = .20 and r = .23, respectively". Detected values: 0.20 (below 120), 0.23 (above 120). Calculation: Average = (0.20 + 0.23) / 2 = 0.215.

section_summary.extract_value: This section discusses the threshold hypothesis, which proposes that high creativity requires at least above-average intelligence (IQ of 120), with intelligence differences becoming irrelevant above this threshold. Several studies are reviewed, some supporting the hypothesis by showing higher correlations between intelligence and creative potential in lower IQ samples (e.g., Fuchs-Beauchamp et al., 1993; Yamamoto, 1964, 1966; Cho et al., 2010) and for crystallized intelligence (Sligh et al., 2005). Conversely, other studies, including a meta-analysis (Kim, 2005) and a large-scale study (Preckel et al., 2006), found no evidence for a threshold effect. Recent investigations into creative achievement (Wai et al., 2005; Park et al., 2007, 2008) also found no intelligence threshold, indicating that intellectual ability predicts creative outcomes even in high-ability groups.
